10628-andrew-golding-a-tale-of-the-great:
Annie E. Keeling's novel Andrew Golding is set during the Great Plague that struck London in 1665. The story is told by Lucia Dacre, who looks back on a time when she and her sister were left in a deserted London house while plague raged through July and August. Their father was dead, and their kinfolk proved little help.

Chapters follow the sisters to Yorkshire, back to London, and at last on a voyage to France in the ship Marie-Royale. Along the way they meet preachers, sailors, and strangers, and Andrew Golding's own fate hangs over their journey. The novel gives readers a moving picture of fear, faith, and family loyalty in a city struck by disease.
1084-recipes-tried-and-true:
The Ladies' Aid Society of the First Presbyterian Church of Marion, Ohio, gathers tried and true recipes from its members, in the style of community cookbooks of the age. Soups, breads, cakes, and preserves fill the pages. Community cookbooks, sold to raise church funds, preserved home cooking across America.

Each recipe was tested in a home kitchen before it was printed, and the book preserves the cooking of small-town Ohio. Food historians and home cooks alike will enjoy its plain, practical voice and its period flavours. The Marion recipes, from Ohio kitchens, show what farm families ate and served guests.
1159-fire-tongue:
Sax Rohmer, creator of Fu Manchu, spins a mystery around Fire-Tongue, a secret eastern cult whose agents strike in London. Nicol Brinn, a cool adventurer with a dark past, stands between the cult and its next victim, while Scotland Yard gropes in the fog. The tale moves from clubs to docks to hidden temples.

Rohmer writes in his usual lurid style, with poison, hypnotism, and exotic menace at every turn. The plot twists fast and the menace never quite lifts. The book suits readers who like pulp thrills and the yellow-peril romances of its age, taken as period pieces.
12078-ireland-historic-and-picturesque:
Charles Johnston's 1902 book Ireland Historic and Picturesque, illustrated, moves from visible and invisible Ireland through the great stone monuments and the cromlech builders to the De Danaans and Emain of Macha. Cuchulain the hero appears in later chapters. Later chapters treat Find and Ossian, the messenger of the new way, and the saints and scholars.

Johnston continues through the raids of the Northmen, the passing of the Norsemen, and the Normans, to the triumph of later invaders and reformers. The book blends archaeology, myth, and history in the manner of early twentieth-century popular scholarship. It presents Ireland's past as a story of monuments, heroes, saints, and invaders that a general reader could follow.
12508-the-meaning-of-good-a-dialogue:
G. Lowes Dickinson's dialogue, third edition 1900, asks what good means, and how people can agree about it. Speakers argue through Book I, starting from the diversity of men's ideas about good. That diversity, at first sight, suggests scepticism, and the dialogue tests whether any firmer ground exists.

A dedication poem about waves on a shore sets a questioning mood, as if human days, like the sea, repeat without clear harbour. Argument, not story, carries the book, with objections raised and answered in turn. Dickinson writes for readers willing to follow a slow, civil debate about value, pleasure and duty.
15097-a-grammar-of-the-english-tongue:
Bound with Samuel Johnson's Dictionary in an 1812 edition, this grammar lays out English in four parts: orthography, etymology, syntax, and prosody. Johnson follows common grammarians, he says, because long use has shown their method clear and full. He keeps received terms rather than inventing new ones.

Short rules and examples guide readers through spelling, word origins, sentence order, and verse sound. The grammar served students who learned English by rule and drill. Today it offers a window onto how the great dictionary maker thought language should be taught, plainly and without needless novelty.
15687-little-essays-of-love-and-virtue:
A set of short essays by Havelock Ellis, the English writer on sex and social life. Ellis, known for his large studies in the psychology of sex, writes here in a gentler, more personal vein. Love, virtue, and the conduct of daily life form his theme. A. and C. Black issued the essays in London for general readers.

Ellis treats love as a force to be understood, not merely praised or feared. He links virtue to kindness, patience, and honest feeling, rather than to strict rules alone. Short pieces move from courtship and marriage to friendship and the duties of parents. The essays still read as humane counsel: clear, calm, and free of preaching, they ask readers to judge love by its fruits in real lives.
16300-the-history-of-emily-montague:
Told wholly in letters, this 1769 novel follows Emily Montague and her circle in Quebec, then still a new British colony. The writers trade news of love, money, and social life, while the wild Canadian scene sits just outside their drawing rooms. One early letter picks Canada over New York for its wilder land and handsomer women.

The book is one of the first novels set in Canada, and its letter form lets each voice speak for itself. Courtship plots cross with talk of rank, land, and the hopes of settlers far from England. For modern readers it gives both a love story and a sharp look at colonial life in the 1760s.
16691-fifth-avenue:
Arthur Bartlett Maurice traces Fifth Avenue's history in this 1918 volume, with drawings by Allan G. Cram. Chapters run from the shadow of the Knickerbockers and the stretch of tradition through glimpses of the sixties. Clubs, literary landmarks, and trails of Bohemia lead on to Murray Hill, the Plaza, and giant strides of commerce. St. Thomas's Church, massive and Gothic, fronts the pictures.

Maurice writes as a New Yorker who loves his city's streets, mixing social history with literary lore. The book suits walkers and readers of New York alike. It remains a rich guide to the avenue's rise from homes to shops and towers.
16870-the-golden-west-boys-injun-and-whi:
William S. Hart wrote this 1922 boys' western, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York with pictures by Harold Cue. Injun and Whitey, heroes of two earlier books, return for a rescue tale. Chapters run from an arrival and a surprise, through mystery and bunk-house talk, to fish-hooks and hooky, a hard job, Felix the Faithless, and a fast ride no gun could stop.

Hart writes for boys in plain, hearty style, with ranch work, jokes, and danger in fair share. The pair's friendship and grit carry them through each scrape. Young readers get a clean, old-style western adventure, full of horses, humor, and a rescue that rewards loyalty and nerve.
18080-normandy-picturesque:
Henry Blackburn wrote Normandy Picturesque, printed in London in 1870 by Sampson Low, in a traveling edition with routes and watering-places. Blackburn, author of books on Spain and the Pyrenees, here guides English readers through the fair French province across the Channel.

Chapters run from Pont Audemer and Lisieux to Caen, Bayeux, St. Lo, Mont St. Michel, Falaise, and Rouen, with Joan of Arc's house among the sights. Blackburn writes with a traveler's ease and an artist's eye. The book still charms as a Victorian guide, full of old towns, green lanes, and Norman stone.
19321-evolution-an-investigation-and-a-c:
Theodor Graebner wrote this 1921 book, Evolution, an investigation and a criticism. He worked from Concordia Seminary, St. Louis. Chapters outline the theory and probe unexplained origins. They cover the testimony of rocks, the fixity of species, and rudimentary organs. They cover instinct, heredity, and a scientific creed outworn. They end with evidences of design and a fatal bias. The book is dedicated to his teacher John Schaller.

Graebner traces descent ideas back beyond Darwin, to Anaxagoras, Aristotle, and Goethe's original plant. Kant's 1790 critique also appears. He argues that speculation on origins long predates the Origin of Species. Readers get a Lutheran scholar's careful, sceptical case against evolution, useful for the history of the debate.
20152-the-winning-clue:
James Hay, Jr. published The Winning Clue in 1919, a detective novel of sudden fright. Bristow leaps up and starts down his porch steps at a run. Two doors away, a frightened girl stands on the porch of No. 5. Though lame, Bristow shows surprising speed as he rushes toward her.

A lame detective makes a fresh hero for a mystery of this era. One winning clue, as the title promises, will crack the case. Hay builds pace from small scenes and sharp turns of talk. Readers get a brisk period mystery with a dogged, unlikely sleuth.
20324-the-outdoor-girls-at-bluff-point-o:
Laura Lee Hope published The Outdoor Girls at Bluff Point in 1920, a tale of a wreck and rescue. Grace Ford drawls as she frees herself from bright cushions. She asks Mollie if Amy has ever said anything important at all. The girls lounge and chat before adventure calls them out.

Bluff Point brings the Outdoor Girls to shore, storm, and a wreck. Hope's series sends its friends camping, boating, and solving small mysteries. Rescue work tests their nerve and teamwork more than talk. Young readers get fresh air, friendship, and a brisk seaside rescue.
206-the-martin-luther-king-jr-day-1995-m:
Editors Judith Boss and John Hamm assembled this memorial issue for Martin Luther King Jr. Day in 1995. The volume gathers classic American writings on slavery, freedom, and Black life, from Sojourner Truth to W. E. B. Du Bois. Frederick Douglass appears several times, with escape and Reconstruction pieces.

Charles W. Chesnutt's conjure tales, Booker T. Washington's awakening, and Chesnutt's Wife of His Youth follow. Harriet Beecher Stowe on Truth and Du Bois on striving round out the set. The issue honors King by returning to the voices that shaped his cause. It serves as a compact anthology for the holiday.
20871-human-foods-and-their-nutritive-va:
Proteins, fats, organic acids, and alkaloids crowd the contents of Human Foods and Their Nutritive Value. Harry Snyder sorts foods by what the body gains from each part. Crude protein, amid compounds, and food value get careful, plain treatment.

Snyder, a Minnesota food chemist, wrote for students of home and farm science. His 1908 book turns lab findings into kitchen and market sense. Tables and tests back each claim about milk, grain, meat, and more. The book marks the rise of nutrition as a science that plain households were urged to learn and use.
21481-true-blue:
True Blue ends his career a warrant officer, and proud of it, in W. H. G. Kingston's tale of that name. Herbert Strang's preface praises its picture of life in the old three-decker navy. The tale covers the wars of the revolutionary age, including the Glorious First of June.

Unlike most boys' heroes, True Blue wins no title and no fortune. He refuses to rise above the class he was born into, by his own choice. Small scenes, like his conduct at a play, make that choice feel true. Kingston closes by saying he always aimed high: at doing his duty.
21720-charlie-to-the-rescue:
Helping others is Charlie Brooke's whole bent of character in this Ballantyne story for young readers. As a small boy in the nursery, Charlie already gets himself into scrapes that hint at his future. His widowed mother watches him with a mix of pride and alarm. In time, rescuing people from trouble and danger grows into his ruling passion.

Ballantyne follows Charlie from childhood into the deeds that give the book its name. Each rescue tests his nerve, his strength, and his kind heart in a new way. The tale is told with warmth and humor. It holds up a brave, selfless boy as a model worth copying.
21970-the-scarlet-plague:
Civilization has fallen and an old man remembers it in Jack London's The Scarlet Plague, published in book form in 1915. The tale opens on a dead railroad embankment swallowed by forest, where a ten-inch tree has burst through a rail. An old man in a goat-skin cap leans on his staff, his beard stained and his eyes shaded by a leaf visor. A boy in a bear-skin leads him along the animal runway.

The old man was once a professor, and he tells the wild boys how the plague emptied the world in days. London wrote one of the first great tales of a ruined future. Its plague year, its empty cities, and its slow forgetting still chill. The story stands near the head of all end-of-the-world fiction.
22415-the-example-of-vertu-the-example-o:
The Example of Virtue is an early English allegory in verse and prose. Its contents list a tournament of virtues for young readers. Four ladies plead at the bar before Justice in its pages.

Each lady claims to be most profitable unto mankind. Justice hears them and gives judgment among the rivals. Afterward, Sapience commands Discretion to lead Youth onward in life. Youth is to marry Cleanness, the King of Love's daughter. Hardiness, sapience, and nature's operations fill other chapters. Such allegory taught conduct through personified virtues in debate. Modern readers get a rare window into Tudor moral teaching for the young.
22776-from-a-terrace-in-prague:
From a Terrace in Prague is a travel book about the Bohemian capital, written from the vantage of a terrace above its roofs and spires. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Prague, before the First World War remade its empire, was still the crown city of Bohemia, layered with Gothic and baroque.

The contents promise the approach as well as the city. They give the routes by which a traveler from the West may reach Prague. A wayside story or two comes along the way. Several very great people appear, and others of a less degree. That dry humor suits a book that treats a city as company. Bridges, castles, and the Vltava carry the narrative once the terrace is reached. It is a civilized souvenir of old Prague.
23229-for-love-of-the-king-a-burmese-mas:
Oscar Wilde's For Love of the King is a Burmese masque, a short courtly play. Its dedication explains how the piece grew out of long, luminous talks with a friend's husband. Those talks took place in the Temple and on the river, while Wilde weighed a different project.

He had been planning a novel as beautiful and intricate as a Persian praying rug. Instead, he hoped this masque caught the atmosphere of those talks and of Burma itself. Readers get a slight, ornamental play: more mood, costume, and courtly feeling than plot, shaped by one of English literature's most famous wits.
24454-across-the-spanish-main-a-tale-of-:
Harry Collingwood wrote this sea adventure from the last years of the sixteenth century, when England fought Spain. Two boys from Devon set out to repair one family's fortunes by hunting Spanish treasure ships. Their voyage carries them across the Spanish Main, the Caribbean coast of South America.

Along the way they are captured by a famous pirate, condemned to be burned by the Inquisition, and saved by escape. A hard cryptogram leads them at last to treasure hoarded by the pirate. Collingwood's tale mixes sea fights, escapes, and code-breaking into a brisk boys' adventure of the Elizabethan age.
25042-color-value:
C. R. Clifford's Color Value, copyrighted in 1907 and printed in a fourth edition by Clifford and Lawton of New York, is a practical manual for interior decoration. It treats light, color, form, proportion, and size as linked conditions, arguing that good rooms come from keeping those five in balance rather than from copying a historic style.

Clifford starts with sunlight, prisms, and the three primary colors, then moves to how colors behave on walls, cloth, and wood. Later sections give working rules for period rooms, from Colonial white to Empire green, and for making small rooms look larger or sunny rooms feel cooler.
25892-eve-to-the-rescue:
Ethel Hueston tells of Eve, a girl who comes in the form of duty and brings only pleasure, in this 1920 novel. Chapters run from defiance of duty and a cote in the clouds to the Irish American League, an inheritance, a wrong adjustment, and painful duty. Eve meets a demonstrator, admits defeat, finds a fixer, and faces a revolt of the seventh step before new light on loyalty dawns.

The tale sparkles at dances, where Eveley Ainsworth in a golden frock dances with solemn Nolan Inglish, her unannounced but accepted sweetheart. Talk over ices turns frank, as a friend asks if Eve means to make a truant husband jealous and offers to play pal. Hueston writes of service as joy, with Marie meeting the secret service and duty at last turning to gladness.
27713-the-elements-of-bacteriological-te:
J. W. H. Eyre, director of the bacteriological department at Guy's Hospital in London, wrote this laboratory guide for medical, dental, and technical students. The second edition, rewritten and enlarged, was published in Philadelphia and London by W. B. Saunders Company in 1913, after a first copyright in 1902.

Eyre opens with laboratory regulations and then works through the methods of bacteriological technique: preparing media, staining, culturing, and examining microbes. Dedicated to his teacher John Wichenford Washbourn, the book trained generations of students in the bench habits behind the new science of germs.
28118-the-great-gray-plague:
Raymond F. Jones wrote The Great Gray Plague, first printed in Analog in February 1962, as a science-fiction tale of a foe that cannot be fought like an army. A dull grey fog, too thin to beat and too wide to escape, threatens a world that depends on clear science. Dr. William Baker, fifty, leads the fight against it.

Baker, a doctor of electronics and chemistry who built key radar work in the Second World War, now holds a top post at the National Bureau of Scientific Development. Jones uses him to ask how science meets a danger with no centre and no shape. The story is a tense, thoughtful piece of early 1960s science fiction.
28593-when-dreams-come-true:
Ritter Brown's When Dreams Come True, published by Desmond FitzGerald in 1912 with illustrations by W. M. Berger, is set in the mountains and plains of Chihuahua. It draws on a Southwest tradition that Montezuma will ride back on an eagle, crowned in gold, to rule again. Captain Forest and his attendant José ride toward Santa Fé for the Fiesta, the Feast of the Corn.

The desert around them holds mesas, sierras, arroyos, and the silence of a land the tale calls forgotten by most. Moonlight dancing, a raised casket, and cries of Madre mia mark later scenes of love and loss. Readers get a romance of legend, landscape, and renewal in the border country.
28855-the-girl-scouts-at-sea-crest-or-th:
Lilian Garis wrote this 1920 Girl Scout story, published by Cupples and Leon in New York. Three girls stand on the beach watching the waves. The chapters that follow bring a bottled warning, a couple of freaks, Captain Dave, crabs and disaster, and a fire at the pier. Later chapters move to the sands, a blanket of fog, the ship Blowell, and the wig wag rescue itself.

Garis, author of The Girl Scout Pioneers and The Girl Scouts at Bellaire, writes scout adventure with sea air and practical heroism. The girls use signals, courage, and teamwork to save the day, in the series' cheerful style. Young readers get a breezy seaside scout tale, with a frontispiece of the captain lifting a girl in his arms on page 161.
29629-the-destroyer-a-tale-of-internatio:
Burton E. Stevenson, author of The Holladay Case and The Marathon Mystery, wrote The Destroyer, a tale of international intrigue. It was printed in 1921 by Dodd, Mead and Company of New York, with copyright in 1913. Its chapters run from the twenty-fifth of September and France in mourning through two great men meeting and the allies at work. The cafe des voyageurs, mysterious signals, and the hut in the grove follow.

Stevenson opens with dark windows showing dawn far distant, and a man turning to sleep again when a sudden remembrance wakes him. The second installation and checkmate close the game. Readers of spy and intrigue fiction will find a brisk, period tale of nations, signals, and secrets.
30062-the-plague:
Teddy Keller imagines a plague that strikes only inside the political borders of the United States, in a short tale printed in Analog in February 1961. Sergeant Major Andrew McCloud, left in charge of a small Pentagon germ warfare office, faces a room full of generals who cannot grasp the crisis. His colonel retired ten days before, his replacement never arrived, and a mysterious epidemic sweeps the country while brass hats demand answers.

Schoenherr drew the pictures, and the story plays its panic for both humor and dread. McCloud and his tiny staff, including Corporal Bettijean Baker, must sort real disease from fear of a germ attack timed to precede invasion. The joke cuts close: a noncom holds the powder keg, while rank alone cannot name what is killing Americans.
30242-prologue-to-an-analogue:
Leigh Richmond plays with Finnagle's Law in a short tale from Analog, June 1961, with pictures by Schoenherr. Its opening newscast, given by Bill Howard of IWC, reports vicious news: a pest sub stuck in the Suez, said to have spread epidemic across Cairo. Howard tells viewers that nations keen to create a crisis may have placed the sub to excuse terror charges, while admitting the sub is real, American made, and the epidemic real indeed.

A United Nations team due in the Canal Zone next day, he says, will find laboratory bacteria carried by the American-made sub, as bad as reported or worse. The tale's twist lies in its title: Finnagle's Law has an inverse, and planned effects do not always land as planned. Richmond turns a Cold War news panic into sly science fiction about blame, proof, and unintended results.
30554-the-adventure-league:
Hilda T. Skae writes The Adventure League, published by Thomas Nelson and Sons in London, Edinburgh, New York, Toronto, and Paris, with a map of Erricha Island. Fifteen chapters open with what happened in Erricha, the pirates' den, a surprise, the compact, and suspense.

Later chapters add a discovery, a siege, a cruise in the Heroic, disappointment, Allan very wise, a near shave, and being surrounded. Andrew MacPeters, being caught, and Hamish to the rescue close the list. A frontispiece notes something familiar in a man's appearance. Skae opens on a bright summer morning, with rocks, heather, green fields, and a dancing sea around a small Scottish island.
31044-the-turn-of-the-road-a-play-in-two:
Rutherford Mayne's play, published in Dublin in 1907 and first produced in Belfast in December 1906 by the Ulster Literary Theatre, is set entirely in the kitchen of a County Down farmhouse. The Granahan family gathers there: farmer William John, his wife, their sons Samuel James and Robbie John, daughter Ellen, and old Thomas Granahan by the turf fire.

Between the two scenes a month passes, and the talk turns on fiddle-playing, farm work, and the choices facing the young. A tramp fiddler and a creamery manager widen the world beyond the kitchen door. Short and warmly observed, the play is a fine example of the early Irish folk drama, rooted in speech, place, and family feeling.
31226-rulers-of-india-albuquerque:
H. Morse Stephens's 1892 volume in the Rulers of India series, edited by Sir William Wilson Hunter and printed at the Clarendon Press, Oxford, tells the life of Afonso de Albuquerque. A list of viceroys and governors of Portuguese India from 1505 to 1580 opens the book, followed by chapters on Albuquerque's predecessors and early career.

The central chapters cover the conquest of Goa, the conquest of Malacca and relief of Goa, and the Red Sea expedition and conquest of Ormuz. They also cover his internal policy, closing with successors from Nuno da Cunha and Dom João de Castro to Dom Constantino and Dom Luis de Athaide. The book remains a compact Victorian life of the viceroy who built Portugal's Asian empire.
31481-tales-from-the-lands-of-nuts-and-g:
Charles Sellers's Tales from the Lands of Nuts and Grapes, Spanish and Portuguese folklore, was published in London in 1888. Sellers states in his preface that he firmly believes the following tales have never before seen the light of publicity. They are, he says, the folklore of Spain and Portugal. He traces the tradition back to Hernando del Castillo, who in 1511 published romances of Spanish chivalry collected from the people. He notes, with regret, that Boccaccio had been most unceremoniously plagiarized by later collectors.

The tales themselves draw on that rich store of song and story, from an inexhaustible mine, as Sellers puts it. Readers will find folk narratives of love, cunning, and wonder, told in English for the first time. The collection is a valuable record of Iberian oral tradition, preserved by a Victorian folklorist who prized originality in a people.
32143-the-romantic-analogue:
W. W. Skupeldyckle's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in September 1953, gives a mathematician a rival for his affections: his own machine. The cover line says Norm Venner doted on his computing machines, until his own device began to flirt with him. Venner is thirty-five, male, with steady brown eyes and a nice smile when he remembers to use it, and a mathematical whiz generally.

Venner built an electronic brain, a calculator that beat him in some ways yet stayed far less shy. Such machines, the story notes, almost always get letter-code names like BINAC, SEAC, and MANIAC, and most count in digits, as if on fingers. Nearly as big as yachts, and costing more, they dominate Venner's fancy. Readers get a comic romance between a man and his machine.
32169-susanna-and-sue:
Kate Douglas Wiggin's Susanna and Sue, illustrated by Alice Barber Stephens, follows a mother and her little daughter on a sad journey to a Shaker settlement. Susanna, called Mardie by her daughter, walks a mile and a half from the station with Sue, after a quiet, pale journey. A boy will bring their little trunk later, so mother and daughter can knock at the visitors' house undisturbed while pleading their case.

Sue dances along the road as a butterfly, in a white cotton dress, straw hat falling off yellow hair, asking again and again if they are nearly there. Susanna knows the road well, having driven it as child and girl. Her grandmother brought her to the settlement once at Sue's age, and again at ten, when the same sweet Eldress received them. Readers get a gentle Wiggin story of refuge, memory, and a mother's hope.
32171-a-discourse-on-the-plague:
Richard Mead's Discourse on the Plague, in a ninth edition corrected and enlarged, was printed in London in 1744 for A. Millar and J. Brindley. Mead, a fellow of the College of Physicians and of the Royal Society and physician to His Majesty, dedicated the work to James Craggs, one of His Majesty's principal secretaries of state. He offers his thoughts on the prevention of the plague, put together at command.

Mead explains that the Lords Justices, in the King's absence, thought action necessary for public safety. Sickness then in France made proper directions needful, to defend the country from such a calamity. He undertook the task at short warning and with little leisure. Readers get an eighteenth-century medical treatise on plague prevention, written by a leading physician for the government of the day.
32448-the-statue:
Mari Wolf's tale, printed in IF Worlds of Science Fiction in January 1953, follows Lewis and Martha, an old couple living in a glassed-in Martian home. Night after night they stay up to watch Earth rise as a clear bright star above the desert horizon, the Morning Star before dawn. Martha, shawl drawn about her knees, trembles with emotion, tiredness, and age as she watches.

Martha tells Lewis she wants to go home, and Lewis knows, after seventy years together, what she means. Earth to them is not a point of light but continents and oceans, a place of memory. Wolf asks where home can be in a universe that keeps changing, and what a lifetime of shared watching means when the watched world grows distant.
32996-the-ten-foot-chain-or-can-love-sur:
This 1920 symposium asks a single playful question: can love survive the shackles, if two people are bound together by a ten-foot chain? An editor dining with four writers tossed the idea into the center of the table, and each writer answered with a tale of his own. Achmed Abdullah, Max Brand, E. K. Means, and Perley P. Sheehan each take the chain and run with it in a different direction.

The four stories range from an Indian jataka to a tale out of the dark, a comic piece, and a story of a princess or a Percheron horse. It shows how one premise can yield romance, humor, and adventure in turn. The book's charm lies in that variety, and in watching four distinct voices test the same bond. It is a light, clever volume, built for readers who enjoy a literary game played well.
33171-one-day-another-a-lyrical-eclogue:
Madison Cawein's lyrical eclogue is a poem in dialogue form, first printed some ten years before this 1901 edition and then reworked at length. Two voices trade lines on days spent among hills, lakes, and woods, musing on youth, love, loss, and the pull of far peaks. Cawein lets nature carry the feeling: light on water, wind in trees, and the slow change of seasons mark each turn of thought.

The poem reads as a song of days rather than a single plot, with short, musical stanzas that rise and fall like talk between friends. Its charm lies in plain images made vivid by sound and rhythm. Readers who like verse that dwells on the outdoors and on memory will find here a gentle, reflective work, shaped by a poet who knew his home ground well.
33381-penny-nichols-finds-a-clue:
Joan Clark's Penny Nichols Finds a Clue, copyrighted in 1936, opens with a warning, a trunk, and an impulsive act, then follows the Molberg gang as Penny turns sleuth. Its chapters move from Susan's misfortune and an awkward situation to a revealing clue, a trap, a vanishing car, a threat, a kidnapping, and a raid. Clark writes for young readers who love a fast, girl-centered mystery.

Penny herself, sharp and brave, drives the tale, with clues that reward close attention. The book's pace is brisk, its villains suitably sly, and its Chicago setting vivid. For fans of series mysteries, Penny Nichols Finds a Clue offers a lively, old-fashioned adventure, where a girl detective outwits grown-up crooks and saves the day.
3363-fennel-and-rue:
William Dean Howells follows a writer's slow success in this novel. Verrian's success arrived neither early nor easily, Howells writes. For years he had sought publication in the leading magazines. Once the editors, who may have favored him all along, took to accepting his work out of conscience.

It was so good in its way, Howells explains, that they could not justly refuse it. That reluctant acceptance drives the novel's comedy of literary life: talent recognized late, and praised as if the delay were the author's fault. Readers who write, or who love writers, will recognize the pattern, and enjoy Howells's gentle revenge on the magazine world.
33867-king-of-camargue:
Jean Aicard writes a novel of the Camargue in this 1901 Philadelphia edition, completely translated by George B. Ives, with etchings by Louis V. Ruet and drawings by George Roux. Dedicated to Émile Trélat, the book opens with Livette and Zinzara, and a woman whose way of looking at people disconcerted them, as if a keen, menacing flame leapt from her eyes. It pierced the being, searched the heart, and left one powerless.

Aicard, poet and idealist, sets his story among the marshes, horses, and herdsmen of the Rhône delta, where a king of the Camargue rules a wild, proud world. The novel blends Provençal color with passionate romance. Readers of French regional fiction will enjoy its vivid landscape, strong heroine, and the contrast between untamed nature and civilized feeling.
4790-half-a-rogue:
Harold MacGrath wrote Half a Rogue, dedicating it to the memory of his mother. Chapter one follows Warrington, whose invariable habit, when no engagement pressed him elsewhere, was to drop into a little restaurant just off Broadway for dinner. Out of the way, the throb of the commercial artery became like the far-off murmur of the sea, restful rather than annoying.

Warrington always dined alone, undisturbed, at a table upstairs, while below the usual dinner crowd gathered till theatre time. Proprietor and waiters had not the slightest idea who he was, knowing him only as a profitable customer who dined there to be alone. Music lured his thoughts astray, since he was fonder of music than of work. In that restaurant he winnowed the day's ideas, revamped scenes, trimmed rough edges of climaxes, and revised or rejected epigrams. Readers get a MacGrath novel opening on a solitary diner.
55928-the-house-of-dreams-come-true:
The House of Dreams-Come-True is a work by Margaret Pedler. It came out in New York in 1919 from Grosset and Dunlap. A poem by the author stands at its front, with a note that Harold Pincott set it to music. The road to the House of Dreams is a strange one, the poem says. Its hills are steep and its valleys deep, and the way is salt with the tears of those who fare on it.

Yet a way there is sure, the poem holds, if the travelers fare straight on through fine days and wet, before the sun has set. The first chapter is called The Wander-Fever. It opens in a great hall whose spaces slope away into deep gloom, with a soft dark that grows deeper by slow degrees, as the tale begins.
5732-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue:
Bunny Brown and His Sister Sue follows a brother and sister through everyday adventures that turn small mishaps into stories. Chapters bring Aunt Lu and a lost ring. Wango the monkey, an empty house, and being locked in follow. Later scenes add drifting in a boat, fishing, a fall in the water, a rescue dog, a trolley ride, and a lemonade stand. Each chapter ends with the children safe and a little wiser.

Readers get gentle, old-fashioned children's fiction, where curiosity leads to scrapes and kindness leads home. Bunny and Sue are brave without being reckless, and adults step in with humor rather than scolding. The book suits early readers and read-aloud families who enjoy a series hero pair whose world is a town, a yard, and a nearby stream.
6571-the-queen-pedauque:
Anatole France tells, through a young cookshop lad, how he learned to read and to live at the sign of Queen Pedauque. The boy turns the spit, meets the learned Abbé Jérôme Coignard, and takes lessons in Latin, Greek, and life itself. His nineteenth birthday brings a new master, a cabalist named d'Asterac, and a move to a strange castle.

There the lad works on old texts, hears gossip, watches a friar and a girl, and feels spring stir his young blood. France mixes learning, hunger, love, and sly humor, with food and books as twin delights. The Queen Pedauque is a rich, witty tale of youth shaped by a priest, a scholar, and a world of old magic.
76470-an-introduction-to-the-theory-of-v:
William Smart wrote this first book on the worth of goods, printed in a fourth shape in 1920. He held the Adam Smith chair of the science of wealth at the University of Glasgow. The book works on the lines of three men of the school of Austria: Menger, Wieser, and Böhm-Bawerk. Its first shape came out in 1891, when the author was fresh from his work on Böhm-Bawerk in English dress.

In a word to the shape of 1910, Smart owns that the thought of that school may have borne him down too much in the first shape. The book had been out of print for long years. He held back from a new print, since a life of work kept him from the later growth of that school. Still, he felt as he had at the start.
77869-eau-de-morgue:
Arthur T. Harris wrote this tale of dread and sleuth work in the worlds to come. A note at its head makes its debt plain. Edgar Allan Poe was a master of the sleuth tale in its first days, and a fine hand at tales of the worlds to come as well. Harris, the note says, has taken a leaf from Poe. He has dared to name his tale Eau de Morgue, in a clear bow to The Murders in the Rue Morgue.

The tale is told by Jan Mystel, who meets the reader face to face at the start. His guest is Detective Sergeant Kurt Milbach, who has come on some charge the teller does not grasp. Mystel owns to a brawl of the night past, but swears his heart is clean, though who knows what his deep mind has been up to.
a-grammar-of-the-english-tongue: Samuel Johnson gives a grammar of the English tongue abstracted from his folio dictionary. The grammar defines its art as using words properly and divides it into orthography, etymology, syntax, and prosody. Johnson's preface to the folio edition stands at the head of the volume. The little grammar remains a classic statement of English usage.
andrew-golding-a-tale-of-the-great-plagu: Anne E. Keeling tells Andrew Golding, a tale of the Great Plague, introduced by Lucia Dacre, who writes the history after her father's death. The story follows kinfolk visiting a household, and how they behaved toward the orphaned children, as plague closes in. Keeling's tale gives young readers a vivid picture of London's terrible year.
bardelys-the-magnificent-being-an-accoun:
Rafael Sabatini's romance of 1905 appears here under its fuller title. The book recounts the strange wooing pursued by the Sieur Marcel de Saint-Pol, Marquis of Bardelys, in Languedoc in the year of the rebellion. A court wager sends Bardelys to win Roxane de Lavédan, whose family stands against the king. The vicomte de Lavédan, a night alarm, and the risen dead thicken the opening movement.

Sheltered after wounds, Bardelys passes as René de Lesperon and inherits the rebel's danger. The king's commissioner hunts him; the tribunal of Toulouse condemns at the eleventh hour. His code is stated to a bristling count: none may impugn his honour without rendering satisfaction, commissioner or not. This is the same novel as the neighbouring Bardelys record, in its Project Gutenberg dress rather than the 2011 reprint.
britannica-1911-achaean-league:
Achaean League was a confederation of the ancient towns of Achaea in Greece, first formed, the entry suggests, as protection against pirates raiding from the Corinthian Gulf. Its twelve cities shared worship of Zeus at Aegium. Dissolved about 288 B.C., the league revived within a decade and grew under the statesmanship of Aratus, until by 228 it embraced Arcadia, Argolis, Corinth, and Aegina.

Federal government is described closely. Member cities kept their own magistrates, assemblies, and courts, yielding only foreign policy and war to the league. A popular assembly of members over thirty met at Aegium each spring and autumn. War with Sparta, Aetolia, and Macedon, and revival under Philopoemen, carry the history forward.
britannica-1911-ague:
Ague, defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, is the common name for a form or stage of malarial disease. The word comes from the Latin acuta, sharp, with febris, fever, understood. An ague fit is the cold, shivering stage of the illness. By loose use, the name also covers any fit of shivering of that kind.

Simple ague keeps much the same character in temperate and tropical climates alike. It can arrive daily, every third day, or every fourth day, forms called quotidian, tertian, and quartan in the entry. From there it may pass into remittent fever, a fever that eases without fully ending. Symptoms and causes are left to the article on Malaria, while brow-ague, a pain over the brow, is sent to the article on Neuralgia.
britannica-1911-albuquerque:
Albuquerque, a city in New Mexico, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county-seat of Bernalillo county, set in the state's centre on the east bank of the Rio Grande at 4,950 feet. Its people grew from 3,785 in 1890 to 11,020 in 1910, making it New Mexico's largest city in 1900. Two main lines of the Santa Fe railway meet there.

Education fills much of the entry. The state university of New Mexico stands east of town. A Methodist industrial school for Mexican girls, a Presbyterian mission school for Mexican boys, and a government Indian training school are listed too. The excellent climate gave the city a reputation as a health resort. Trade ran through stock-yards and shops shipping livestock, hides, and wool. The largest works was the American Lumber Company's plant, sawing white pine from the Zuni mountains.
britannica-1911-apologue:
An apologue is a short fable or tale with a hidden sense. It is meant to carry a moral truth or a useful lesson in a pleasant form. The tale of Jotham in the Book of Judges is one of the best known. Horace wrote one of a city rat and a field rat. Livy tells one of the belly and its members, spoken by Menenius Agrippa. The tales of Aesop are the most famed.

The term fits best a story whose actors are beasts or things of nature. An apologue always holds a moral sense, which a fable need not hold. It is as a rule dramatic in form. Some have called it a satire in action. It differs from a parable in key ways. A parable can be true, but an apologue gives beasts our speech and feelings. It thus lacks real truth by its very nature.
britannica-1911-avenue:
Avenue, from the French verb avenir, to come to, means a way of approach. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry gives its chief sense as the entrance road to a country house, lined with rows of trees on each side, the trees themselves forming the avenue.

By modern times the word had spread widely as a name for town streets, with or without trees. Fifth Avenue in New York and Shaftesbury Avenue in London stand as the entry's examples. So a term born from great houses and planted rows became ordinary street naming in large cities.
britannica-1911-baroque:
Baroque is a technical term used chiefly for architecture, furniture, and household decoration. It seems to come from Spanish: a barrueco is a large pearl of irregular shape. For a time the word stayed inside the jeweller's craft, naming such uneven stones, before it spread to design at large.

The style it names is the more extravagant fashion common in the first half of the 18th century, above all in Italy and France. Everything in it is fantastic, grotesque, florid, or incongruous: irregular shapes, forms without meaning, and an utter lack of restraint and simplicity. The 1911 Britannica entry adds that the word suggests much the same order of ideas as rococo, its lighter cousin.
britannica-1911-battue: Battue, from the French battre, to beat, is a sporting term explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In shooting, a battue is the beating of game out of its cover. The birds or animals are driven within range of the sportsmen's fire and shot as they break out. By likeness the word is also used for any slaughter of crowds that cannot defend themselves, a sense that carries the hunting term into accounts of war and massacre.
britannica-1911-ben-venue:
Ben Venue is a mountain in south-west Perthshire, Scotland, ten miles west of Callander. Its two chief peaks stand 2,393 and 2,386 feet high. Standing near the south-east shore of Loch Katrine, its bold outline is among the best-known sights of the Trossachs.

Sir Walter Scott set the Coir-nan-Uriskin, the “Goblin’s Cave,” at the mountain’s north base in The Lady of the Lake. Just south of the cave runs the Bealach-nam-Bo, the “Cattle Pass.” Highland raiders once drove stolen herds through it into the safety of the Trossachs. The pass is little visited, yet the entry judges its scenery the grandest in the whole district.
britannica-1911-benue:
Benue is a river of West Africa, the largest and most important stream feeding the Niger. It runs over eight hundred miles, in the main from east to west, from its source in the mountains of Adamawa to its meeting with the Niger. Few African rivers match its length among the Niger’s branches.

Through the Tuburi marshes a water link joins the Benue system to the Shari and Lake Chad system, so that in flood the two great basins touch. The entry is very short: a name, a source, a course, a junction, and that one marsh link eastward. For the river it feeds, the reader is sent to the article on the Niger itself.
britannica-1911-bernard-mountague:
Mountague Bernard (1820–1882), an English lawyer of Huguenot descent, was educated at Sherborne and Trinity College, Oxford, and called to the bar at Lincoln's Inn in 1846. The 1911 Britannica entry centres on his election in 1852 to Oxford's new professorship of international law and diplomacy, attached to All Souls College.

Beyond Oxford he served on royal commissions, went to Washington in 1871 as a high commissioner and signed the Treaty of Washington, and assisted at the Geneva arbitration in 1872. He was an original member of the Institut de Droit International in 1873. His best-known book treated British neutrality during the American Civil War.
britannica-1911-bisque:
Bisque is a French word of unknown origin, once spelled bisk in English. In games it names a handicap gift given to the weaker player. In tennis a bisque is one point the receiver may claim at any time in a set. In croquet and golf it is one extra stroke, taken at choice during a game. The gift is spent once, at the moment it helps most. That is the sporting sense the 1911 Britannica entry gives first.

Cookery holds a second, unrelated sense of the word. There a bisque is a thick soup, made especially of crayfish or lobsters. The entry is a short note of a few lines covering both uses. It gives the word's French source and its old English spelling. No recipes or dates are supplied in the text. One short French word thus does two different jobs, at table and on court.
britannica-1911-bouhours-dominique:
Dominique Bouhours (1628–1702) was a French Jesuit critic who set rules for pure French style. Born in Paris, he entered the Society of Jesus at sixteen and lectured on literature at the Clermont college in Paris and on rhetoric at Tours. He then tutored the duke of Longueville's two sons and was sent to Dunkirk to serve English Catholic refugees.

Amid mission work he kept publishing books. His Entretiens d'Ariste et d'Eugène (1671), talks on the French language, was printed again and again across Europe. Other works include Doutes sur la langue française (1674), lives of Ignatius Loyola and Francis Xavier, and a French New Testament (1697). His habit of alternating worldly and devout books drew the joke that he served the world and heaven by half-years, the entry records.
britannica-1911-brogue:
Brogue carries two senses that share nothing but the sound. First, it names a rough shoe of raw, untanned leather, from the Gaelic brog, a shoe, worn in the wilder parts of Ireland and the Scottish Highlands. Footwear for rough country is the whole of that first sense, and the entry gives it in one line.

Second, brogue names a dialect accent or way of speaking, of uncertain origin, used especially of the Irish accent in speaking English. No root is offered for this second sense, in contrast to the clean Gaelic source given for the shoe. The brief notice simply sets the two side by side: a Highland and Irish shoe of raw hide, and the Irish lilt in English speech that took the same word.
britannica-1911-carducci-giosue:
Giosuè Carducci (1836–1907) was an Italian poet. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and work. He was born at Val-di-Castello, in Tuscany, on 27 July 1836. His father was a physician of an old Florentine family. The father had been jailed for his part in the 1831 revolution. Carducci had a good education and began as a teacher. He soon gave private lessons at Florence instead.

At Florence he joined a circle of young patriots. In literature they sought to overthrow romantic taste. They aimed at a return to classical models in verse. Those aims stayed the mainsprings of Carducci's poetry. In 1860 he became professor at Bologna. His defiant Hymn to Satan astonished the public in 1865. Levia Gravia followed in 1868 and headed a school. The Decennalia, Nuove Poesie and Odi Barbare came after. The article follows his fame to the head of Italian letters.
britannica-1911-claque:
Claque, from the French claquer, to clap the hands, is an organised body of professional applauders in the French theatres. Hiring applause was common in classical times, and Nero had five thousand soldiers chant praise when he acted. A 16th century French poet, Jean Daurat, revived the idea by giving free tickets to men who promised approval of his play. Not until 1820 did a M Sauton systematise the claque with a Paris office.

By 1830 the claque was a regular institution, run under a chef de claque who judged where efforts were needed and started each demonstration. Kinds of claqueur fill the closing detail, commissaires who learn the piece and praise it between acts, and rieurs who laugh loudly at the jokes. Pleureurs, generally women, feign tears with handkerchiefs to their eyes. Chatouilleurs keep the audience in good humour, while bisseurs clap and cry bis.
britannica-1911-clue:
Clue, or clew, from the Old English cluwe, was originally a ball of thread or wool, the thread of life which the Fates spin for every man, in the fable. Ordinary figurative meaning flows directly from a famous story, as the entry tells it. Theseus was guided through the labyrinth by the ball of thread held by Ariadne at the entrance. From that thread a clue became a piece of evidence leading to discovery in common speech.

A sign pointing to the right track carries the same figurative sense, of a thread that leads out of confusion. No other meanings are set out, and no examples from law, hunting or letters are offered in this notice. Ball of thread, the Fates' spinning, Ariadne's gift and Theseus in the labyrinth make the chain whole. The modern detective sense descends from that mythic thread.
britannica-1911-epilogue:
Epilogue is the appendix or supplement to a literary work, and in particular to a drama in verse, from the Greek name for the closing part of a speech. As in Shakespeare's Midsummer Night's Dream, the epilogue was generally the apology for a play. It was a final appeal for the audience's good nature, meant to ward off attack. 

Among the ancients the form was barely grown: the last speaker stepped forward with “Vos valete, et plaudite, cives,” or the single word “Plaudite!” The entry calls the epilogue as a literary kind almost wholly English, and rare even in Shakespeare. Ben Jonson made it a regular feature of his drama and may almost be said to have founded its tradition. He used it either to assert a play's merit, as in Cynthia's Revels of 1600, or to beg pardon for its faults, as in Volpone of 1605.
britannica-1911-eubulus-demagogue:
Eubulus of Anaphlystus was an Athenian demagogue of Demosthenes' time and that orator's steady opponent. He helped secure the acquittal of Aeschines, once his own clerk, on the embassy charge. He cared little for war and at first backed peace at any price. His strength lay in administration, above all finance. He is said to have raised the revenues and done real service. Yet he also used the state's resources to build his own power.

His law made it death to propose spending the Theoric Fund on war. The entry judges that the rule served his popularity, not the state. As an envoy he let Philip of Macedon win him over. After his death, before 330, Athens gave him special honours. None of his speeches survives. Aristotle names one speech against Chares, and Theopompus had written his life.
britannica-1911-florez-enrique:
Enrique Florez (1701–1773) was a Spanish historian, born at Valladolid on 14 February 1701. At the age of fifteen he joined the order of St Augustine. He later taught theology at the university of Alcala. He put out a course of theology in five volumes from 1732 to 1738. After that he gave his life to the study of the past. His first fruit in that field was the Clave Historial of 1743.

That book was of the same class as the French Art de vérifier les dates, and it came before that work by some years. It went through many editions. In 1747 the first volume of his España Sagrada came out. That vast set on the church past of Spain won a name all over Europe. Twenty-nine volumes came out in his life, and the work went on after his death.
britannica-1911-fugue:
Fugue, from the Latin fuga, flight, is in music the mutual pursuit of voices or parts. Up to the late 16th century the name covered two forms. Fuga ligata, the exact restatement of a leading part by a following voice, came to be called canon. Freer work in the same style was the fuga ricercata or ricercare, a title Bach still used.

The entry sends the full treatment to Contrapuntal Forms and defines terms here. A countersubject is the material kept against later entries of the subject. Episodes are the passages between entries, usually grown from the subject matter. Stretto is the overlapping of subject and answer, shown in Bach Magnificat. The split between real and tonal fugue is judged a small detail of how the answer is fitted to the dominant. The article closes with Milton lines on the resonant fugue.
britannica-1911-value:
Value, from the French value and the Latin valere, means worth in common use. In the study of wealth it has a special sense, and that sense is the subject of this article. The article rests its account, in part, on the views of J. S. Mill. Mill, it says, drew into his book on political economy near all that key past work held. Later gains in the field have most often come by way of critique or growth of his view.

That holds with most force for the theory of value itself. Mill had so well worked through the mass of past thought on the point that he could open with a bold claim. He held that the laws of value held no point left for a writer of his day, or of days to come, to clear up.
bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue:
Bunny Brown and His Sister Sue, by Laura Lee Hope, opens the Bunny Brown series for young children, in a New York edition of 1916. Hope, who also wrote the Bobbsey Twins books, introduces two small children whose days turn ordinary errands into adventures. Florence England Nosworthy supplied the illustrations, and the contents promise a visit from Aunt Lu in the very first chapter.

A lost ring, a monkey named Wango, and an empty house carry the early chapters. Bunny and Sue get locked in, drift off in a boat, and watch Sue fall in and be pulled out with a rescue dog's help. A trolley ride loses them properly before they are found, and a goat gives Sue one more scare. Each scrape ends safely at home, which is exactly the rhythm its first readers wanted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-afonzo-de-alb:
Afonzo de Albuquerque, also called Dalboquerque and surnamed the Great, died at Goa on 16 December 1515. Second son of Villaverde's lord Gonzallo de Albuquerque, he attached himself to Portugal's king. He travelled to Otranto alongside Alphonso V in 1480 and first sailed to the far East in 1503, back in Lisbon by 1504. Tristan de Cunha's 1506 sailing for India found Albuquerque among his officers.

He planned to monopolize East Indian trade for Portugal by excluding Venetians and Saracens, and therefore sought mastery of the Red Sea. For that end he seized Socotra and attacked Ormuz, landing on 10 October 1507 and raising fortifications. After Almeida's return in 1509, Albuquerque succeeded him as viceroy. He destroyed Calicut in January 1510, took Goa in March, lost it, retook it in November, and held it for Portugal thereafter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-adrian-for:
Blessed Adrian Fortescue, knight and martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born about 1476 to the Salden branch of the Devonshire Fortescues, he was executed in 1539. A country gentleman of his age, he followed the king to war in France in 1513 and 1522, attended court, and served as justice of the peace.

Knighted in 1503, present at the Field of the Cloth of Gold in 1520, he became a Knight of St. John in 1532. Kinship with Anne Boleyn, his mother's grand-niece, first helped then doomed him, as Henry VIII's treason charges swept up loyal men. The entry presents a gentleman caught in a king's terror.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-nicho:
Nicholas of Flue, the Swiss hermit called Brother Klaus, left wife, ten children, and public office for a hermit's life. He lived twenty years in a ravine chapel without food or drink, as civil and church investigators confirmed. Born near Sachseln in 1417, he farmed and soldiered in Swiss wars. He married Dorothy Wyssling and served as councillor and judge.

With his wife's consent he withdrew in October 1467 to the Ranft gorge. Visitors from across Europe sought his counsel there. He was credited with saving Sarnen from fire by prayer in 1468. His advice helped settle Swiss disputes, and he died on his seventieth birthday, 21 March 1487, still in his hermitage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capefigue:
Capefigue was a French historian born at Marseilles in 1802 who died at Paris in December 1872. Trained in law, he turned to journalism and edited the Legitimist Messager des Chambres. He served briefly in the Foreign Ministry and lost his post in the July Revolution. He remained a strong Royalist who later backed the Orleanists and then Napoleon.

A prolific writer, he produced histories judged somewhat superficial yet firm in devout Catholic conviction. Above all stand a four-volume history of Philip Augustus and a ten-volume history of the Restoration. That second work treats the fall of the elder Bourbon branch. Church-history works such as a life of Vincent de Paul sit beside a four-volume survey of the early Church and a historical novel on James II at Saint-Germain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catafalque:
A catafalque is the raised, tomb-like structure used at funeral offices when the body is absent. Draped in black cloth bearing a cross, it stands just outside the sanctuary. It becomes the focus of the absolution rite. Candles burn around it. It is sprinkled with holy water and incensed, receiving the same honors the corpse would receive if present.

The article sets out the practical rules for its use, including where the cross-bearer and celebrant stand during the absolution. Where no catafalque can be had, a square black cloth before the lowest altar step serves instead. It also notes the grander funeral monuments of earlier times, such as the one fellow artists raised for Michelangelo in Santa Croce, Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cenni-di-petr:
Cenni di Petro Cimabue was a Florentine painter born in 1240 and dying after 1301, famed as the founder of Italian painting and as Giotto's reputed master. Vasari opens his life with a flood of disasters overwhelming Italy. Art and artists alike had vanished, until Cimabue was born at Florence to light the way toward painting. Greek settlers in Florence were said to be his masters. He soon surpassed them, and Charles of Anjou is said to have visited his studio.

All this later research has disproved, crediting it to Vasari's pride in Florence, his home city. The supposed dark age of the thirteenth century is no longer believed: Pisa, Lucca, and Pistoia already had cathedrals, and Assisi's basilica was rising. The works in Assisi showing the Last Ends, of savage grandeur, may or may not be Cimabue's, but they are certainly the work of a great artist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-de-la:
Charles de la Rue was one of the great Jesuit orators of seventeenth-century France, born at Paris in 1643 and dead there in 1725. He entered the novitiate in 1659 and later taught humanities and rhetoric. While still young he won attention with verses celebrating Louis XIV's victories. Corneille translated it and gave it to the king, saying his own work did not match the young Jesuit's original. He also wrote tragedies, brought out an edition of Virgil, and composed Latin poems.

His superiors several times refused him permission to go to Canada and instead assigned him to preaching. His orations for the Dukes of Burgundy and Luxemburg, and for Bossuet, rank as masterpieces. So do his sermons on public calamities and on the dying sinner. He spent three years preaching missions among the Protestants of Languedoc.

Charles de Larue was a Benedictine scholar born at Corbie in 1685 and dead at St. Germain-des-Près in 1739. He showed early talent for languages and a religious vocation, took the Benedictine habit at St. Faro in Meaux. After studying philosophy and theology, he went to Paris in 1712 to assist Dom Bernard de Montfaucon in literary work. Montfaucon soon valued his young assistant and charged him with a new edition of Origen.

Larue worked with energy: printing began in 1725, and eight years later two volumes appeared, dedicated to Pope Clement XII. Larue also showed that two works passed off as Origen's, against Marcion and against heresies, were falsely ascribed. A stroke of paralysis ended his labours while material for two more volumes stood ready, and his nephew Vincent de Larue, of the same congregation, edited them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosmas-of-pra:
Cosmas of Prague, a Bohemian historian born about 1045, wrote the first history of his people. Schooled at Prague and Liege, he entered church life young, married while still a minor cleric, and rose to dean of St Vitus cathedral chapter. He travelled with Bohemia's bishops and enjoyed the trust of its rulers.

His Latin Chronica Bohemorum runs in three books from the earliest times to 1125, drawing on popular tradition for the early age and on witnesses, documents, and his own experience later. Truthful, careful to separate certainty from rumour, and vivid in portraiture, he earned the nickname Herodotus of Bohemia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-decalogue:
A short scriptural entry explains the Decalogue, from Greek words for ten and word, as the collection of precepts on two stone tables given by God to Moses on Sinai. Its injunctions and prohibitions appear in Exodus chapter 20 and Deuteronomy chapter 5. Differences in style between the two accounts touch reasons given for precepts, not the precepts themselves.

The Catholic division and ordering follows Saint Augustine, while the common Protestant division seems to follow Origen. Origen read Exodus 20:3-6 as two commandments, leaving verse 17 as one, to keep the total ten. Catholic practice reverses this. Readers are referred to the fuller article on the Commandments of God for the precepts themselves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dubuque:
Dubuque is an archdiocese set up on 28 July 1837 and raised to an archbishopric in 1893. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry maps it across northern Iowa, an area of more than eighteen thousand square miles. The city stands picturesquely on the Mississippi beneath bluffs rising three hundred feet, many crowned with Catholic institutions and fine homes. It takes its name from Julien Dubuque, a Canadian who mined lead and traded with the Indians there from 1788 to 1811.

The first white visitors to Iowa were the Jesuit Marquette and the Franciscan Hennepin, and later missionaries followed from the east. The entry draws on lives of Bishop Loras and histories of Iowa Catholics to trace a frontier church grown into an archdiocese. His grave, marked by a cross, now bears a rugged tower of native stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugene-melchi:
Eugene-Melchior, Vicomte de Vogue, critic, novelist, and historian, was born at Nice on 25 February 1848 and died in Paris on 24 February 1910. An illustrious Vivarais family, which sent many men to Church and army in the Middle Ages, was his descent. Versailles gave him his classical studies, and Grenoble gave him law studies. He enlisted as a private when the Franco-Prussian war broke out, and bravery won him the military medal.

After the war he entered the diplomatic career. Constantinople took him as an attaché of embassy in 1873, Egypt in 1875, and Saint Petersburg after that. In 1878 he married a Russian lady, Miss Annenkof. Literature claimed him after he resigned four years later. From 1893 to 1896, however, he represented Ardèche in the Chamber of Deputies. The French Academy elected him in 1888.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filioque:
Filioque means and from the Son in the Latin Nicene Creed. It states the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son together, as one Principle. The East rejected it, helping to cause the great Greek schism. Great councils from Lateran IV to Florence declared it a dogma of faith.

Scripture calls the Spirit both the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. The Son sends the Spirit, just as the Father sends the Son. Sending implies procession, theologians argue, and never inferiority. Photius denied the procession and opposed the insertion of Filioque into the Creed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-benno:
Francis Bennon Ducrue, born at Munich on 10 June 1721 and dead there on 30 March 1779, was a Jesuit missionary in Mexico and California. Of French parents, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1738. Ten years later he was sent to California, where he laboured with zeal until the order's expulsion in 1767, when he stood as superior of all the California missions. He submitted without complaint to the expulsion decree and even helped the royal commission enforce it.

The Jesuits left California carrying only their clothes and a few books, all the wealth they took from seventy years of mission work. Ducrue returned to his native land and wrote in Latin an account of his journey from California through Mexico to Europe in 1767, translated into German and French. He also supplied specimens of California native languages, preserving fragments of tongues that might otherwise have vanished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-german-cathol:
The German Catholic League, founded at Munich on July 10, 1609, bound Catholic states to defend their faith and the empire's peace. Duke Maximilian of Bavaria had opposed such a confederacy three years earlier. By 1607 he urged it so each member might know how far to rely on the others. The Protestant Union's birth in May 1608 spurred him, and talks with spiritual electors and Catholic states ran through the Ratisbon Diet and Andernach conferences of 1608.

At Munich, Augsburg, Constance, Passau, Ratisbon, and Würzburg allied for nine years. Members would not war on each other, disputes went to arbitration or imperial law, and an attacked member drew the League's arms or legal aid. Maximilian presided, with Augsburg, Passau, and Würzburg's bishops as councillors. Mainz, Cologne, and Trier's electors adhered on August 30, having proposed a 20,000-man confederate army. Cautious, dilatory states kept the structure thinner than its foundation promised.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hartman-von-a:
Swabian knight Hartmann von Aue, a Middle High German epic poet and singer of love songs dead between 1210 and 1220, was unusually learned for a layman of his day. He could read and write and was versed in French, Latin, and the literature of his time. After his lord's death he joined a crusade, though whether that of 1189 or 1197 is uncertain.

His fame rests on four epics: Erec. This brought Arthurian romance into German letters through the clash of love and knightly honour. Iwein tells of a hero who neglects his wife, goes mad, and wins her back. Gregorius is a medieval Oedipus who atones and becomes pope. In Poor Henry a maid's offered sacrifice is refused and the leprous lord is healed, leaving polished courtly verse as a model for later poets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heroic-virtue:
Heroic virtue is a degree of goodness far above the ordinary, the standard the church uses when judging a candidate for beatification. The word hero once meant a warrior or demigod famed for bravery, and St. Augustine first gave the pagan title to Christian martyrs. Later use spread it to confessors whose virtues and good works greatly outran ordinary good people's.

Benedict XIV, whose chapters on the subject are classical, describes heroic virtue as acting with uncommon promptness, ease, and pleasure from supernatural motives, with self-denial and full mastery of natural inclinations. Such virtue becomes a second nature, making easy acts that would daunt most people. It belongs, the entry says, only to souls purified from worldly attachment and anchored in love of God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ibague:
Ibagué is a suffragan diocese of Bogotá in Colombia, formed when the wide diocese of Tolima was suppressed by decree in June 1900 and split into Ibagué and Garzón. Ibagué covers the two provinces forming the republic's northern and central portions. Its city, San Bonifacio de Ibagué, capital of Tolima department, lies on a fertile plain about sixty miles west of Bogotá, over four thousand feet above sea level.

The city, seat of the bishopric, dates from 1550 and briefly served as republican capital in 1854. Its first bishop, Ismaël Perdomo, born in 1872, was elected in April 1903, consecrated at Rome in June, and preconized later that month. The diocese counts about two hundred and fifty thousand Catholics, and its cathedral, still building, was to be dedicated to the Immaculate Conception.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-balue:
Jean Balue, a French cardinal born about 1421 in Poitou and dead in 1491 at Ripatransone, climbed by clever intrigue from law graduate to royal favourite. After serving bishops of Poitiers and Angers, he won the trust of Louis XI, who made him almoner in 1464 and showered him with abbeys and the bishopric of Evreux.

Balue then pushed his first patron out of Angers and took that see himself in 1467, gaining the cardinal's hat the same year at the king's urging. Two years later he was seized for high treason with the bishop of Verdun, a fall that matched the ruthless methods of his rise. His career shows how closely church office and royal politics were bound in late medieval France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lambert-le-be:
Lambert Le Begue, a priest and reformer of twelfth-century Liege, was a poor man's son, ordained by a route of doubtful regularity and probably parish priest of St. Christophe. He preached against clerical abuses and vices, attacking simony, the ordination of priests' sons, and customs around baptism and Mass.

Some views, on the day of rest and Masses for the dead, look suspect. Yet he drew a popular following and put the Life of the Virgin, Acts, and Paul's Epistles into the vernacular with commentaries, now lost. He likely organized the Beguines, whose name probably comes from begue, stammerer, his own nickname. Condemned for heresy and jailed despite appeal to Rome, he escaped to the antipope Callistus III and likely died at Liege in 1177.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-bourdal:
Louis Bourdaloue was the great French preacher called king of preachers and preacher of kings, born at Bourges in 1632 and dead at Paris in 1704. He joined the Jesuits at fifteen, taught philosophy and moral theology, and was turned to preaching after chance sermons showed his gift.

From the provinces in 1665 he moved to Paris in 1669. He preached there for thirty-four straight years, at the height of his powers to the end. Friend and rival of Bossuet, he differed in method. Where Bossuet swept wide, Bourdaloue reasoned close and plain, holding court and common folk alike with moral sermons that still rank among France's finest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquette-lea:
Marquette League was a lay society founded in New York in May 1904 by Rev. H. G. Ganss of Lancaster, Pennsylvania.  It aimed to work with church authorities to keep the faith among Catholic Indians in the United States and convert those still pagan.

It also aimed to fund mission schools, new missions, chapels, and trained catechists, and to better Indians' spiritual and material lot by every lawful means. In its first six years to 1910 it built chapels at Holy Rosary and St Francis in South Dakota, for Moquis in northern Arizona, and for Winnebagoes in Nebraska. It built two more on Fort Berthold Reservation in North Dakota. It kept several catechists in the field and sent clothing, money, and Mass offerings yearly to mission schools and priests. It worked in harmony with Washington's Bureau of Catholic Indian Missions across almost every state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martinique:
Martinique was a diocese in the French Lesser Antilles, 380 square miles in area. Columbus discovered it in 1493, France colonised it about 1625, England held it from 1762 to 1783 and again in 1792, 1802, 1809, and 1815, and it returned to France in 1818. Its name comes from the Carib word Madinima.

On Good Friday 1640 Jesuits Bouton and Hempteau sailed for Martinique and founded its celebrated Jesuit mission. Fellow Jesuits Ceubergeon and Gueimu were slain there in 1654 by revolting Caribs. A 1707 memoir on catechising Negro slaves shows the mission's work. In 1753 Pere de Lavalette became superior general and prefect apostolic. His business dealings later drew violent attacks on the Society, though Rochemonteix proved he acted without fellow missionaries' or superiors' knowledge. When the Second Republic freed slaves in 1848, prefect apostolic Castelli hailed an era of light and evangelical regeneration. The diocese, created 27 September 1850, counted 170,000 people and forty-six priests, and suffered Mt Pelee's 1902 eruption destroying St Pierre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mensa-mensal-:
Mensa, Latin for table, means in church language that share of a church's property set aside to meet the costs of the prelate or the community serving the church. It is run at the will of one or the other. The word first meant a meal table, then by extension the means of sustenance and all resources for personal support. One who lives at another's cost and table is his commensal.

In a cathedral served by both bishop and chapter, the bishop's mensa stands apart from the chapter's. The first yields revenues the prelate enjoys, the second those the chapter enjoys. The capitular mensa now rests chiefly in individual property. The old common mensa has nearly everywhere split among canons, each holding a personal share called a prebend. Likewise, abbeys in commendam split an abbatial mensa for the abbot from a conventual mensa for the community.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mozambique:
Mozambique, the former official name for Portugal's East African possessions opposite Madagascar, stretches some 1,200 miles from Cape Delgado to Delagoa Bay. It is the second largest Portuguese colony at about 293,000 square miles with between two and three million people. Its low, marshy coasts are cut by rivers ending in muddy deltas choked with sand.

Between the Limpopo and the Zambezi delta the land is barren, lagoonal and malarial, and the tsetse fly bars cattle raising. Between the Zambezi and Rovuma the soil is fertile, enriched by yearly floods. The coastal climate is torrid and changeable, cooling inland as the ground rises. The entry covers the colony's history from early Portuguese settlement, its trade and missions, and the Catholic Church's organisation there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-penance-as-a-:
Penance as a virtue means the inward sorrow and resolve that stand behind every outward act of atonement. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry separates the virtue from the sacrament, the canonical punishment, and the works of satisfaction, which other articles treat. All four share one centre: the sinner must repent and, as far as possible, repair the wrong done to divine justice.

Its core act is hatred of one's own sin because it offends God, not merely regret for the pain or disgrace that followed. A firm purpose to amend matters too, but the entry insists such a purpose means little without sorrow for sins already committed. Scripture anchors the argument, from Ezekiel's call to a new heart through John the Baptist, the Prodigal Son, the Publican, and the Magdalen who washed out her sins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prague:
Prague is an archdiocese in Bohemia. From about the mid sixth century, Slav tribes pushing into Bohemia drove the Marcomanni to the land's edge. In 845 Czech princes and their warriors came to Louis the German's court at Ratisbon and were baptized on 13 January by the Bishop of Ratisbon. The first duke surely Christian is his son Spitigniew, who in 895 bound himself to Arnulf of Carinthia.

Bishop John set up the Inquisition's court at the Council of Vienna's wish. Within a year it handed fourteen heretics to the State, who burned them at the stake, and the bishop sent the Inquisitors packing and freed their prisoners. Church wealth peaked under Charles IV. Schooled at the French court, Charles kept his teacher Peter de Rosières, now Pope Clement VI, close. In 1344 Charles won a Bull lifting Prague to an archbishopric, with Olmütz among its suffragans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priests-commu:
The Priests' Communion League is a priestly association raised at Rome on 20 July 1906, at San Claudio, under the Fathers of the Blessed Sacrament. Pius X lifted it to an archconfraternity ten days later. Its aim is to spread daily and frequent Communion among the faithful, in line with the Decree Sacra Tridentina Synodus of 20 December 1905.

To join, a priest must have his name written in the league's register. He pledges himself, though with no bond of conscience, to push the Decree's observance with zeal by prayer, preaching, and the press. He must also take the monthly Emmanuel. Members start by teaching the folk what the Eucharist is and what it works, as sacrifice, as God's real presence among us, and as food for our souls. They teach that daily Communion lawfully asks no more than yearly Communion: grace's state and right intention.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priests-eucha:
Paris saw the Priests' Eucharistic League raised by Pierre-Julien Eymard, who founded the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament. As early as 1857 he felt the need to draw clergy to closer converse with the sacramental Lord. Only in 1867 did the plan of a distinct confraternity ripen, and the Curé d'Ars stood among the first to enroll. The association took its present shape in 1879 and won Leo XIII's approval on 25 January 1881. Six years later, on 16 January 1887, Cardinal Parocchi, cardinal vicar, definitively approved and canonically raised it in Rome's church of San Claudio.

The Archconfraternity of the Most Holy Sacrament at San Claudio is the league's canonical centre, though its central office stands in Brussels. The confraternity's first aim is the frequent and long worship of the Blessed Sacrament by priests. Since Christ, truly God with us in the Eucharist, longs for priests to come oft into His presence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-senanque:
Sénanque, a Cistercian monastery on the Sénancole stream in the diocese of Avignon, became the cradle of the modern Cistercians of the Immaculate Conception. Alfant, Bishop of Cavaillon, and Raymond Bérenger II, Count of Provence, founded it in 1148 with Saint Bernard's backing. The first monks came from Mazan abbey under Peter, their first abbot. Extreme poverty marked the start, until the lords of Simiane built a spacious monastery.

Bernard's name drew postulants fast, and the community soon passed one hundred members. It founded Chambons in 1152. Later it weakened, fell into commendam in 1509 with barely a dozen monks, and was suppressed in the Revolution with only one monk left. In 1854 Abbé Barnouin bought the well-preserved abbey and set up a community under a middle rule, stricter than the common observance but milder than La Trappe.
